comments.why_zh: 深入探讨 simple 与 easy 以及隐式状态。
comments.quote_zh: Rich Hickey 有一个关于这个想法很棒的演讲
comments.text_zh: 把所有那些状态都记在脑子里很难。我认为，由于 FP 的局限，新程序员更容易推理程序，老实说，也更容易学会编程。新开发者不必像使用命令式语言那样事无巨细地管理计算机。例如，SQL 不是 FP，但想想有多少业务分析师，如果他们必须写命令式程序从某种数据存储中取数据，日子会难过得多。我认为归根结底是 simple 与 easy 之别。命令式编程在最开始非常 easy，但并不 simple。因为程序里有这么多隐式状态，随着程序增长，它会变得非常非常 complex。它不再 simple。Rich Hickey——Clojure 的创造者——有一个很棒的演讲详细探讨了这个想法。[VIDEO]
comments.text: Keeping track of all that state in one’s head is hard. I think because of the limitations of FP it’s much easier for new programmers to reason about programs and honestly, learn to program. New developers don’t have to micromanage the computer, the way that the would with an imperative lang. For example, SQL isn’t FP, but think about the number of business analysts whose lives would be more difficult if the had to write imperative programs to fetch data from some sort of data store. I think what in comes down to is simple vs easy. Imperative programming in the very very beginning is easy, buts not simple. Because there’s all this implicit state in your program, as the program grows it becomes very very complex. It’s no longer simple. There’s this really great talk about this idea by rich hickey, the creator of clojure, that dives into this in detail. [VIDEO]

comments.story_title: I'm dialing back my LLM usage
comments.text_zh: 我觉得 LLM 让很多开发者忘掉了《Simple Made Easy》里的那些教训：[VIDEO] LLM 似乎特别擅长复现那种经典的“泥球”（Ball of Mud）——既没法重构，也没法理解。用简单的组件去和别的简单组件交互、从而产出一个复杂功能，这里面有很大的威力。同时每个组件都容易理解、容易调试、也容易预测它的性能。诀窍在于想清楚怎么把你那个复杂问题拆解成这些简单组件以及它们之间的交互。我想，等 LLM 真正把这项技能练好了，那才是我们真的不再需要开发者的时候。
comments.text: I think LLMs have made a lot of developers forget the lessons in "Simple Made Easy": [VIDEO] LLMs seem to be really good at reproducing the classic Ball of Mud, that can't really be refactored or understood. There's a lot of power in creating simple components that interact with other simple components to produce complex functionality. While each component is easy to understand and debug and predict its performance. The trick is to figure out how to decompose your complex problem into these simple components and their interactions. I suppose once LLMs get really good at that skill, will be when we really won't need developers any more.

comments.why_zh: 提供了 braided、complected 这种复杂性概念的来源。
comments.text_zh: 构建用户体验本质上属于最困难的软件工程工作之一。它难，不是因为现有工具做得差（尽管大多数确实差），而是因为核心问题极其复杂（采用 Rich Hickey [1] 对“复杂”一词的理解，例如 braided、intertwined、complected 等）。为了构建用户体验，我们起初有一些信息，这些信息常常（当然并非总是）看起来既 simple 又 easy（即 unbraided 且可理解）。但随后我们必须把这些信息投射到二维（或三维）平面上，并管理它随时间变化的状态。一切就在这里崩坏。我们通常试图管理一棵非常宽、非常深、定义松散的状态树，并试图即时且随时间反映任意数量的用户交互和变更。我们的工具（编程语言、UI 工具包、操作系统等）中，恰好零个能强有力地支持管理随时间变化，使这类问题在呈现、使用、验证或变更时变得快速、稳定或令人愉快。我喜欢原帖作者展示的 Performance、Adaptability 和 Velocity 三角。自 2011 年以来，我一直和团队用类似概念来框定问题，我称之为“Fast, Stable and Delightful”。我的论点是，我们需要在活动以及产出的结果中平衡这三个要求。这种平衡极难达成，维持起来更难。
comments.text: Building user experiences is inherently some of the most difficult software engineering there is. It's not difficult because the existing tools are poorly made (though most of them are), it's difficult because the core problem is extremely complex (in the Rich Hickey [1] sense of the word, e.g., braided, intertwined, complected, etc.). In order to build a user experience, we start with some information that can often (though certainly not always) appear both simple and easy (i.e., unbraided and comprehensible). But then we must create a projection of that information onto a 2D (or 3D) plane and manage it's changing state over time. This is where everything falls apart. We're usually trying to manage a very wide, very deep, loosely defined tree of state and we're trying to reflect an arbitrary number of user interactions and mutations instantly, and over time. Exactly zero of our tools (programming languages, UI toolkits, Operating Systems, etc.) have strong support for managing change-over-time in a way that makes this type of problem fast, stable or enjoyable to present, use, verify or mutate. I love that the OP showed the triangle of Performance, Adaptability and Velocity. I've been framing a similar concept with teams since 2011 which I refer to as, "Fast, Stable and Delightful." comments.quote_zh: 你也许会说，你正在把事物“complecting”到一起
comments.text_zh: 复杂性：缠绕在一起的事物。你可以数事物，也可以数缠绕。当一组事物的缠绕（甚至打结）比另一组少时，它就更简单。当你拉拽某物时，如果它通过缠绕与其他事物相连，你就在处理复杂性。当你有意把事物交织在一起时，你就在制造复杂性。你也许会说，你正在把事物“complecting”到一起，一旦完成，它们就“complected”在一起了。这与编程中从最小细节（比如状态——相较于更简单、无时间性的不可变值，状态是值与时间更复杂的缠绕）到最大的模块化问题（模块化是由更小事物组成的系统的一种属性；当你能够断开这些事物而无须把它们彼此解开缠绕时，你就实现了一个更简单的设计）都相关。这与容易或困难是分开的，尽管可以断言更简单的系统往往更容易修改，因为你不一定需要同时处理那么多缠绕在一起的事物。但这不是必然的，因为程序员会学习并越来越擅长处理复杂事物，以至于它们可能感觉相当容易；我们也热衷于制造工具，试图去驾驭复杂性的来源，无论是问题域固有的，还是我们不必要地加诸自身的；而一旦你学会其中一些工具，修改真正复杂的系统也可能相当容易。复杂的事物也可能非常有用，从 ti
comments.text: Complexity: things twisted together. You can count the things, and count the twists. When a set of things has fewer twists (or even knots) than another set of things, it's simpler. When you pull on something, if it's attached to other things by twists, you are dealing with complexity. When you intentionally entwine things, you are creating complexity. You might say you are "complecting" things together, and once done they are "complected" together. This is relevant from the smallest details of programming like state (being a more complex twist of value and time, compared to simpler immutable values that are timeless) to the largest issues of modularity (being a property of systems composed of smaller things; when you can disconnect such things without needing to untwist them from each other, you have achieved a simpler design). This is separate from being easy or hard, though one could assert that a simpler system will tend to be easier to change, because you don't necessarily have to deal with as many things twisted together at the same time. But this isn't a given, because we programmers learn and get better at complex things such that they can feel quite easy, and we also love making tools to try and wrangle sources of complexity, either those inherent to a problem domain, or those we unnecessarily inflict on ourselves, and it can be quite easy to make changes to really complex systems once you've learned some of these tools. comments.author: zahlman
comments.story_title: Solving the Wrong Problem
comments.text_zh: 我想说，如今更该怪的是库和框架，而不是语言。我们并没有创造出恰当的、优雅的 DSL。但更重要的是，我们仍然指望人们通过继承库里的 class——也许还继承好几层——来换入换出功能。我们明明可以直接把函数当作一等对象来用，却反而得去理解代码与数据那种不自然的混杂；这种混杂基于对问题域（而不是解决方案域）里某个所谓概念的“建模”，而它本身几乎没什么道理。就像 Rich Hickey 解释过的（[VIDEO]），事物之所以变复杂，是因为你把它们 complect（纠缠）在一起了。精心编写的 Python 或 JavaScript 能给你很多 APL / LISP 的感觉。当然，不是元编程那部分。但 LISP 里很多这种东西依赖于 homoiconicity，而它正是让这门语言“普通开发者用不了”的最大原因之一。
comments.text: I would argue that nowadays the libraries and frameworks are more to blame than the languages. We aren't creating the right elegant DSLs. But more importantly we're still expecting people to inherit from library classes — perhaps multiple levels deep — to swap functionality in and out. We could just use functions as first-class objects but instead we have to understand this unnatural intermingling of code and data that's based on "modeling" a supposed concept in the problem domain (rather than the solution domain) that barely makes any sense in and of itself. Like Rich Hickey explained ( [VIDEO] ), things become complex because you complect them. You can get a lot of APL / LISP feeling out of carefully written Python or JavaScript. Not the metaprogramming stuff, sure. But a lot of that in LISP depends on homoiconicity, which is one of the biggest things making the language "not usable by average developers".
